questions.question: Refer to the parabolic trajectory of a projectile launched with velocity u at angle θ. At the highest point of its flight (H_max), what are the vertical and horizontal velocity components?

options.A: Vertical velocity v_y = 0; Horizontal velocity v_x = u cos θ
options.B: Both vertical and horizontal velocities are zero
options.C: Vertical velocity v_y = u sin θ; Horizontal velocity v_x = 0
options.D: Both components equal u sin θ

questions.solution:
**Correct Answer: (A)**

**Mechanics:** Throughout projectile flight, horizontal acceleration is zero, so $v_x = u \cos \theta$ remains constant. At peak height $H_{max}$, vertical velocity $v_y = 0$.

# 🎯 Motion in a Plane — Class 11, Chapter 4
### Complete NEET Preparation Guide

---

## 1. 🔷 Core Concept & Definition

**Motion in a Plane** means motion in **two dimensions** — along both X-axis and Y-axis simultaneously.

> Think of it this way: Motion in a **line** = 1D. Motion in a **plane** = 2D. Motion in **space** = 3D.

The most important idea here is the **principle of independence of motion**:
> *"The horizontal and vertical components of motion are completely independent of each other."*

This single principle is the **backbone** of the entire chapter.

### Types of Motion in a Plane:
| Type | Example |
|------|---------|
| Projectile Motion | Ball thrown at an angle |
| Circular Motion | Stone tied to a string |
| Relative Motion in 2D | River-boat problems |

---

## 2. 📐 Key Formulas

### 🔹 A) Vector Basics (Foundation)

A vector quantity has **both magnitude and direction.**

**Position vector:**
$$\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j}$$

**Displacement vector:**
$$\Delta\vec{r} = \vec{r_2} - \vec{r_1} = \Delta x\hat{i} + \Delta y\hat{j}$$

**Magnitude of a vector:**
$$|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$$

**Direction (angle with X-axis):**
$$\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{A_y}{A_x}\right)$$

---

### 🔹 B) Projectile Motion (Most Important for NEET!)

When a body is thrown at angle **θ** with the horizontal with initial velocity **u**:

| Quantity | Formula |
|----------|---------|
| Horizontal velocity | $u_x = u\cos\theta$ (constant throughout) |
| Vertical velocity | $u_y = u\sin\theta$ (changes due to gravity) |
| Velocity at time t | $v_x = u\cos\theta$, $v_y = u\sin\theta - gt$ |
| Horizontal displacement | $x = u\cos\theta \cdot t$ |
| Vertical displacement | $y = u\sin\theta \cdot t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$ |
| **Time of flight** | $T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$ |
| **Maximum height** | $H = \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$ |
| **Horizontal range** | $R = \frac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$ |
| **Maximum range** | $R_{max} = \frac{u^2}{g}$ at θ = 45° |

> 📌 **Special case:** Angles **θ** and **(90° − θ)** give the **same range** but **different heights**.
> Example: 30° and 60° give same R, but H is different.

**Equation of trajectory** (path of projectile):
$$\boxed{y = x\tan\theta - \frac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}}$$
→ This is a **parabola** — directly confirm in MCQs asking "what is the shape of path?"

---

### 🔹 C) Circular Motion (Uniform)

| Quantity | Formula |
|----------|---------|
| Angular velocity | $\omega = \frac{\theta}{t} = \frac{2\pi}{T}$ |
| Linear velocity | $v = r\omega$ |
| Centripetal acceleration | $a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r$ |
| Centripetal force | $F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r$ |
| Time period | $T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}$ |

> ⚠️ **NEET Trap:** Centripetal force is NOT a new force — it is provided **by** tension, gravity, friction, normal force, etc.

---

### 🔹 D) Relative Motion in 2D

$$\vec{v}_{AB} = \vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B$$

> Used in **river-boat problems**, **rain-man problems**

**River-boat crossing:**
- To cross in **minimum time** → boat heads **perpendicular** to river
- To cross with **minimum drift** → boat heads at an **angle upstream**

---

## 3. 📋 Common NEET Question Patterns

### Pattern 1: Range & Height Problems
> *"A projectile is fired at 30°. Find range, max height, time of flight."*
→ Direct formula application. Just plug in.

### Pattern 2: Same Range Angles
> *"Two projectiles have same range. If one is fired at 20°, what is the angle of the other?"*
→ Answer: **70°** (since θ and 90°−θ give same range)

### Pattern 3: Horizontal Projectile
> *"A ball is thrown horizontally from height H. Find time to reach ground and range."*
→ Here θ = 0°, so $u_y = 0$
- Time: $H = \frac{1}{2}gt^2 \Rightarrow t = \sqrt{\frac{2H}{g}}$
- Range: $R = u \cdot t$

### Pattern 4: Velocity at a Point
> *"Find velocity of projectile at highest point."*
→ At highest point, **vertical velocity = 0**, so only horizontal component remains = **u cosθ**

### Pattern 5: Circular Motion
> *"A car takes a circular turn of radius r at speed v. Find centripetal acceleration."*
→ $a = \frac{v^2}{r}$

### Pattern 6: Rain-Man Problems
> *"A man walking east at 3 m/s. Rain falls vertically at 4 m/s. At what angle should he hold umbrella?"*
→ Use vector subtraction, find resultant direction.

---

## 4. 🧠 Memory Tips & Analogies

### 🎯 Analogy for Projectile Motion:
> Imagine you throw a **cricket ball** at an angle. Your friend standing beside you on a **moving train** sees the ball go straight up and come straight down — that's the vertical component. But you standing on ground see it travel horizontally too. **Both views are correct because the motions are independent.**

### 🔑 Memory Tricks:

**"RHAM"** for projectile formulas:
- **R** = Range → $\frac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$
- **H** = Height → $\frac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g}$
- **A** = Angle for max range → **45°**
- **M** = Max range → $\frac{u^2}{g}$

**For complementary angles (same range):**
> "**30-60, 20-70, 15-75**" — always pairs that add up to 90°

**Centripetal vs Centrifugal:**
> Centripetal = **real force** (acts inward, in inertial frame)
> Centrifugal = **pseudo force** (appears outward, in rotating frame)
> NEET mostly asks about **centripetal** only.

---

## 5. 📝 Example Problem with Solution

### ❓ Problem:
*A ball is projected with velocity 20 m/s at an angle of 30° with the horizontal. Find:*
*(a) Maximum height reached*
*(b) Time of flight*
*(c) Horizontal range*
*(Take g = 10 m/s²)*

---

### ✅ Solution:

**Given:**
- u = 20 m/s
- θ = 30°
- g = 10 m/s²

**Step 1: Resolve initial velocity**
$$u_x = u\cos 30° = 20 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 10\sqrt{3} \approx 17.3 \text{ m/s}$$
$$u_y = u\sin 30° = 20 \times \frac{1}{2} = 10 \text{ m/s}$$

**Step 2: Maximum Height (H)**
$$H = \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g} = \frac{(20)^2 \times \sin^2 30°}{2 \times 10}$$
$$H = \frac{400 \times \frac{1}{4}}{20} = \frac{100}{20} = \boxed{5 \text{ m}}$$

**Step 3: Time of Flight (T)**
$$T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g} = \frac{2 \times 20 \times \sin 30°}{10} = \frac{2 \times 20 \times 0.5}{10} = \frac{20}{10} = \boxed{2 \text{ s}}$$

**Step 4: Horizontal Range (R)**
$$R = \frac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g} = \frac{(20)^2 \times \sin 60°}{10}$$
$$R = \frac{400 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{10} = \frac{200\sqrt{3}}{10} = 20\sqrt{3} \approx \boxed{34.6 \text{ m}}$$

**Verification check:** Notice that at θ = 60°, the range would be the same (34.6 m) but the height would be different

# Projectile Motion — Complete NEET Guide
### Class 11 | Chapter 4: Motion in a Plane

---

## 1. 🎯 Core Concept & Definition

**Projectile motion** is a type of motion where an object moves under **two simultaneous influences**:
- **Horizontal direction** → No force → Constant velocity (uniform motion)
- **Vertical direction** → Gravity acts → Acceleration = g downward (non-uniform motion)

> **Golden Rule:** Horizontal and vertical motions are **completely INDEPENDENT** of each other.

### The Fundamental Setup:
When a body is projected at angle **θ** with the horizontal with initial velocity **u**:

```
         ↑ uy = u sinθ           • ← highest point (vy = 0)
         |                      / \
         |                    /     \
         |                  /         \
         |    θ            /             \
         |_______________/________________\____→
         O    ux = u cosθ                  R (Range)
```

**Initial velocity components:**
| Component | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Horizontal (uₓ) | u cosθ |
| Vertical (uᵧ) | u sinθ |

---

## 2. 📐 Key Formulas (Absolutely Must Memorize!)

### 🔵 At Any Instant (t):

| Quantity | Formula |
|----------|---------|
| Horizontal velocity | vₓ = u cosθ (**constant**) |
| Vertical velocity | vᵧ = u sinθ − gt |
| Horizontal displacement | x = u cosθ · t |
| Vertical displacement | y = u sinθ · t − ½gt² |
| Resultant speed | v = √(vₓ² + vᵧ²) |

---

### 🔴 The Three Master Formulas:

$$\boxed{T = \frac{2u\sinθ}{g}}$$ ← **Time of Flight**

$$\boxed{H = \frac{u²\sin²θ}{2g}}$$ ← **Maximum Height**

$$\boxed{R = \frac{u²\sin 2θ}{g}}$$ ← **Horizontal Range**

---

### 🟢 Equation of Trajectory (Path Shape):

$$\boxed{y = x\tanθ - \frac{gx²}{2u²\cos²θ}}$$

> This is the **equation of a parabola** → Proves projectile follows a **parabolic path**

---

### ⭐ Special Cases (High-Yield for NEET!):

| Condition | Result |
|-----------|--------|
| Maximum Range | θ = **45°** → R_max = u²/g |
| Complementary angles | θ and (90°−θ) give **same range** |
| At highest point | vᵧ = 0, only vₓ = u cosθ remains |
| T and H relationship | H = gT²/8 |
| Range and Height | R = 4H cotθ |

---

## 3. 🔥 Common NEET Question Patterns

### Pattern 1: Finding Range or Height
*"A ball is projected at 30° with speed 20 m/s. Find horizontal range."*
→ Directly apply R = u²sin2θ/g

### Pattern 2: Complementary Angles
*"Two projectiles have same range. If one is projected at 30°, find the other angle."*
→ Answer: **60°** (because 30° + 60° = 90°)

### Pattern 3: Trajectory Equation
*"Find the angle of projection if horizontal range = 4 × maximum height"*
→ Use R = 4H → u²sin2θ/g = 4 × u²sin²θ/2g → **θ = 45°**

### Pattern 4: Velocity at Highest Point
*"A projectile is fired at 60°. Find KE at highest point if initial KE = E"*
→ At top, v = u cos60° = u/2 → KE = ½m(u/2)² = E/4

### Pattern 5: Time of Flight Problems
*"Two balls are thrown horizontally from heights h₁ and h₂. Find ratio of times."*
→ T = √(2h/g) → T₁/T₂ = √(h₁/h₂)

### Pattern 6: Horizontal Projectile
*"Ball rolled off a table of height 20m with speed 5 m/s. Find range."*
→ First find T using h = ½gT², then R = uT

---

## 4. 🧠 Memory Tips & Analogies

### The "Busy Road" Analogy:
> Imagine throwing a ball while sitting in a car moving at constant speed. The ball goes **forward** (because of car's speed) and **falls down** (because of gravity). These are INDEPENDENT — exactly like projectile motion!

### Memory Tricks:

**"STC" for the three formulas:**
- **S**in²θ → Height (H)
- **T**wo × sinθ → Time (T) [2u sinθ/g]
- **C**os appears in Range [sin2θ = 2sinθcosθ]

**For Maximum Range:**
> "**Forty-Five to go farthest** — golfers know this!" → θ = 45°

**Complementary angles give same range:**
> "30° and 60° are a couple — they share the same range!"

### Quick Cross-Check Method:
At θ = 45°: H = R/4 (Height is always ¼ of Range at 45°)
Use this to verify your answer in MCQs!

---

## 5. 📝 Example Problem with Solution

### Problem:
A cricket ball is hit at 30° above the horizontal with an initial speed of 40 m/s. Calculate:
(a) Maximum height reached
(b) Time of flight
(c) Horizontal range
*(Take g = 10 m/s²)*

---

### Solution:

**Given:**
- u = 40 m/s, θ = 30°, g = 10 m/s²
- sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = √3/2, sin 60° = √3/2

---

**(a) Maximum Height (H):**

$$H = \frac{u²\sin²θ}{2g} = \frac{(40)² × (0.5)²}{2 × 10}$$

$$H = \frac{1600 × 0.25}{20} = \frac{400}{20}$$

$$\boxed{H = 20 \text{ m}}$$

---

**(b) Time of Flight (T):**

$$T = \frac{2u\sinθ}{g} = \frac{2 × 40 × 0.5}{10} = \frac{40}{10}$$

$$\boxed{T = 4 \text{ s}}$$

---

**(c) Horizontal Range (R):**

$$R = \frac{u²\sin 2θ}{g} = \frac{(40)² × \sin 60°}{10} = \frac{1600 × \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{10}$$

$$R = \frac{800\sqrt{3}}{10} = 80\sqrt{3}$$

$$\boxed{R ≈ 138.6 \text{ m}}$$

---

### ✅ Quick Verification:
- R = 4H cotθ = 4 × 20 × cot30° = 80 × √3 ✓ **(Matches!)**

---

## 🏆 NEET Exam Quick-Revision Card

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          PROJECTILE MOTION SUMMARY          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  T = 2u sinθ / g                            │
│  H = u² sin²θ / 2g                          │
│  R = u² sin2θ / g                           │
│                                             │
│  Max Range → θ = 45°  → R = u²/g            │
│  Same Range → Complementary angles          │
│  At top → only horizontal velocity          │
│  Path → Parabola                            │
│  Horizontal → uniform motion (no force)     │
│  Vertical → uniformly accelerated           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

> 💡 **NEET Tip:** In NEET, approximately **1-2 questions** appear from projectile motion every year. These are usually **formula-based and straightforward** — if you memorize the 3 master formulas and the special cases, you can solve them in under 60 seconds!

[NEET 2022 | Physics]

A projectile is thrown with velocity v making angle θ with the horizontal. The range of the projectile is same when the angle of projection is:
questions.solution:
# Correct Answer: **(C) 90° − θ**

## Step-by-Step Solution

**Range Formula:**
$$R = \frac{v^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$$

**For Same Range:**

For two angles of projection to give the same range:
$$\sin 2\theta_1 = \sin 2\theta_2$$

**Using Sine Property:**

The sine function satisfies: sin A = sin B when A + B = 180°

Therefore:
$$2\theta_1 + 2\theta_2 = 180°$$
$$\theta_1 + \theta_2 = 90°$$

**Finding the Complementary Angle:**

If first angle is θ:
$$\theta + \theta_2 = 90°$$
$$\theta_2 = 90° - \theta$$

## Verification with Examples

| Angle 1 | Angle 2 | sin 2θ₁ | sin 2θ₂ | Range |
|---------|---------|---------|---------|--------|
| 30° | 60° | sin 60° | sin 120° | Same ✓ |
| 20° | 70° | sin 40° | sin 140° | Same ✓ |
| θ | 90°-θ | sin 2θ | sin(180°-2θ) | Same ✓ |

## Why Other Options are Wrong

- **(A) 45° + θ**: No special property; different ranges
- **(B) 180° − θ**: Would give negative or >90° angles; physically unrealistic
- **(D) 90° + θ**: Would exceed 90° for most values; gives different range

## Key Concept to Remember

**Complementary Angles in Projectile Motion:** Two angles θ and (90° − θ) always produce the same range. This is called the "supplementary angle" property of projectile motion.

# Motion in a Plane — Class 11, Chapter 4
## Complete NEET Study Guide

---

## 1. 🧠 CORE CONCEPT & DEFINITION

**Motion in a plane** means motion in **two dimensions** — an object moves along both the **X-axis and Y-axis simultaneously**.

> The key idea: **Treat X and Y directions as completely INDEPENDENT of each other.**

### Building Blocks You Must Know First:

### 📌 Vectors vs Scalars
| Feature | Scalar | Vector |
|---|---|---|
| Has magnitude only | ✅ | ❌ |
| Has direction too | ❌ | ✅ |
| Examples | Speed, distance, mass | Velocity, displacement, force |

---

### 📌 Vector Addition — Triangle & Parallelogram Law

**Triangle Law:** If two vectors are represented as two sides of a triangle taken in order, the **third side (closing side, taken in reverse)** represents their resultant.

**Parallelogram Law:**
$$\vec{R} = \vec{A} + \vec{B}$$

$$|\vec{R}| = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta}$$

**Direction of resultant:**
$$\tan\alpha = \frac{B\sin\theta}{A + B\cos\theta}$$

> 🔑 **Special cases:**
> - θ = 0° → R = A + B (maximum)
> - θ = 180° → R = |A − B| (minimum)
> - θ = 90° → R = √(A² + B²)

---

### 📌 Resolution of Vectors (Most Important for NEET!)

Any vector can be broken into **two perpendicular components:**

$$\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j}$$

$$A_x = A\cos\theta, \quad A_y = A\sin\theta$$

$$|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$$

---

### 📌 Position & Displacement Vector

$$\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j}$$

$$\vec{\Delta r} = \vec{r_2} - \vec{r_1} = (x_2 - x_1)\hat{i} + (y_2 - y_1)\hat{j}$$

---

### 📌 Velocity & Acceleration in 2D

$$\vec{v} = v_x\hat{i} + v_y\hat{j}$$

$$\vec{a} = a_x\hat{i} + a_y\hat{j}$$

Each component follows the **same 1D equations independently**.

---

## 2. 🔑 KEY FORMULAS

### ⭐ PROJECTILE MOTION (Most tested in NEET!)

An object thrown at angle **θ** with horizontal, with initial speed **u**:

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| Horizontal velocity | $u_x = u\cos\theta$ (constant throughout) |
| Vertical velocity | $u_y = u\sin\theta$ (changes due to gravity) |
| Time of flight | $T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$ |
| Maximum Height | $H = \dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$ |
| Horizontal Range | $R = \dfrac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$ |
| Maximum Range | $R_{max} = \dfrac{u^2}{g}$ (at θ = 45°) |
| Velocity at any time t | $v_x = u\cos\theta$, $v_y = u\sin\theta - gt$ |
| Equation of trajectory | $y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$ (parabola!) |

> 🎯 **Golden Facts:**
> - Range is same for **θ** and **(90° − θ)** → e.g., 30° and 60° give equal range
> - At maximum height, **only horizontal velocity exists** (vertical = 0)
> - Horizontal acceleration = **0**; Vertical acceleration = **g (downward)**

---

### ⭐ UNIFORM CIRCULAR MOTION

Object moves in a circle with **constant speed but changing velocity direction:**

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| Angular velocity | $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi f$ |
| Linear speed | $v = r\omega$ |
| Centripetal acceleration | $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r$ |
| Centripetal force | $F_c = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r$ |
| Time period | $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$ |

> ⚠️ **Common misconception:** Centripetal force is **NOT a new force** — it is the **net force directed towards center** (could be tension, gravity, normal force, etc.)

---

### ⭐ RELATIVE VELOCITY IN 2D

$$\vec{v}_{AB} = \vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B$$

"Velocity of A **with respect to** B"

---

## 3. 📋 COMMON NEET QUESTION PATTERNS

### Pattern 1: Range & Angle Problems
> *"At what angle should a ball be projected to get maximum range?"*
> *"Two projectiles have same range — find ratio of heights"*

### Pattern 2: Time of Flight Comparisons
> *"A ball is projected horizontally from a cliff of height h. Find time to hit ground."*
> → Use only vertical: $h = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$

### Pattern 3: Velocity at a Point
> *"Find speed/angle of projectile at maximum height"*
> → Speed = $u\cos\theta$ (only horizontal component remains)

### Pattern 4: Circular Motion — Centripetal Force Source
> *"A stone tied to string moves in circle — what provides centripetal force?"*
> → **Tension in string**

### Pattern 5: Vector Addition
> *"Two forces of equal magnitude act at angle θ — find resultant"*
> → $R = 2F\cos(\theta/2)$

### Pattern 6: Relative Velocity
> *"Rain falling vertically at speed v. Man walks at speed u. At what angle should he hold umbrella?"*

---

## 4. 💡 MEMORY TIPS & ANALOGIES

### 🎯 For Projectile Motion:
> **"Horizontal is the LAZY component — it never changes speed. Vertical is the HARDWORKING one — gravity constantly pulls it down."**

### 🎯 For Range Formula:
> Remember **sin2θ** → Range is maximum at **2θ = 90° → θ = 45°**
> **"45 is the magic angle for maximum throw!"**

### 🎯 For Complementary Angles:
> **"30° and 60° are twins — they always give the same range!"**
> Similarly: 20° & 70°, 15° & 75°

### 🎯 For Circular Motion:
> **"Centripetal = Centre-seeking. Like Earth always 'seeks' the Sun — gravity IS the centripetal force for orbital motion."**

### 🎯 Vector Components Trick:
> **"The component ALONG the angle uses cos θ (it's closer/adjacent), the one ACROSS uses sin θ"**

---

## 5. 📝 EXAMPLE PROBLEM WITH SOLUTION

### Problem:
> A ball is projected with a velocity of **20 m/s** at an angle of **30°** with the horizontal. Find:
> **(a) Maximum height reached**
> **(b) Horizontal range**
> **(c) Speed at maximum height**
> *(Take g = 10 m/s²)*

---

### Solution:

**Given:**
- u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°, g = 10 m/s²

**Step 1: Find components**
$$u_x = u\cos 30° = 20 × \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 10\sqrt{3} \text{ m/s}$$

$$u_y = u\sin 30° = 20 × \frac{1}{2} = 10 \text{ m/s}$$

---

**Step 2: Maximum Height (H)**

$$\boxed{H = \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g} = \frac{(20)^2 × \sin^2 30°}{2 × 10}}$$

$$H = \frac{400 × \frac{1}{4}}{20} = \frac{100}{20} = \mathbf{5 \text{ m}}$$

---

**Step 3: Horizontal Range (R)**

$$\boxed{R = \frac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g} = \frac{(20)^2 × \sin 60°}{10}}$$

$$R = \frac{400 × \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{10} = \frac{200\sqrt{3}}{10} = \mathbf{20\sqrt{3} \approx 34.6 \text{ m}}$$

# Vector Addition — Analytical Method
### Class 11 | Chapter 4: Motion in a Plane | NEET Physics

---

## 1. 🧠 Core Concept and Definition

When two or more vectors act simultaneously on a body, we need to find their **resultant** (net effect). The **analytical method** uses **mathematics (trigonometry + algebra)** to find the exact magnitude and direction of the resultant — unlike the graphical method which is approximate.

### The Setup:
Consider **two vectors A and B** acting at a point, with an angle **θ between them**.

```
        B
       /
      /  θ
     /___________
          A
```

We use the **Parallelogram Law of Vector Addition** as the basis, then apply trigonometry to solve analytically.

---

## 2. 📐 Key Formulas

### ✅ Magnitude of Resultant R:

$$\boxed{R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta}}$$

Where:
- A = magnitude of vector **A**
- B = magnitude of vector **B**
- θ = angle between the **two vectors**

---

### ✅ Direction of Resultant (angle α with vector A):

$$\boxed{\tan\alpha = \frac{B\sin\theta}{A + B\cos\theta}}$$

> α is the angle the resultant makes **with vector A**

---

### ✅ Special Cases Table:

| Condition | θ | Resultant R |
|-----------|---|-------------|
| Vectors in **same direction** | 0° | R = A + B (Maximum) |
| Vectors **perpendicular** | 90° | R = √(A² + B²) |
| Vectors in **opposite direction** | 180° | R = |A - B| (Minimum) |
| **Equal vectors** at angle θ | θ | R = 2A cos(θ/2) |

---

### ✅ Component Method (for multiple vectors):

Break each vector into **X and Y components**, then add:

$$R_x = A_x + B_x = A\cos\theta_1 + B\cos\theta_2$$
$$R_y = A_y + B_y = A\sin\theta_1 + B\sin\theta_2$$
$$R = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2}, \quad \tan\alpha = \frac{R_y}{R_x}$$

---

## 3. 🎯 Common NEET Question Patterns

### Pattern 1: Direct Formula Application
> "Two forces of 3N and 4N act at 90°. Find resultant."
→ Simply apply R = √(A² + B²) → R = √(9+16) = **5N**

---

### Pattern 2: Finding Angle for Given Resultant
> "Two equal forces F act at angle θ. Resultant = F. Find θ."
→ Use R = 2F cos(θ/2)
→ F = 2F cos(θ/2) → cos(θ/2) = 1/2 → θ/2 = 60° → **θ = 120°**

---

### Pattern 3: Maximum and Minimum Resultant
> "Two vectors have resultant maximum = 18 and minimum = 6. Find magnitudes."
- R_max = A + B = 18
- R_min = A - B = 6
- Solving: **A = 12, B = 6**

---

### Pattern 4: Component-Based Problems
> "A vector of 10N makes 30° with X-axis. Find components."
→ Ax = 10 cos30° = 5√3 N, Ay = 10 sin30° = 5 N

---

### Pattern 5: Perpendicular Components (very NEET-favorite!)
> "Resultant of two vectors is perpendicular to one of them."
→ Use condition: **A + B cosθ = 0** (since tanα → ∞ means denominator = 0)

---

## 4. 💡 Memory Tips and Analogies

### 🗺️ Analogy: GPS Navigation
If you walk **3 km East** then **4 km North**, you don't travel 7 km total — you travel **5 km** in a diagonal direction (Northeast). This is exactly what vector addition calculates!

---

### 🧲 Memory Trick for formula:
**"Root of A-square, B-square, Two-AB-cosθ"**
```
R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cosθ)
     ↑    ↑      ↑
  first  second  middle term
  vector vector  (interaction term)
```
> Think of it as the **Law of Cosines** from geometry — it IS the same formula!

---

### 🔑 Key Reminders:
- θ is the angle **between the two vectors**, NOT with the axis
- When θ = 90°: the middle term (2AB cosθ) = **zero**, so it simplifies to Pythagoras
- R is always between |A-B| and (A+B)

---

## 5. 📝 Example Problem with Solution

### Problem:
Two vectors **P = 6N** and **Q = 8N** act at a point making an angle of **60°** with each other. Find:
(a) Magnitude of resultant
(b) Angle it makes with vector P

---

### Solution:

**Given:**
- P = 6N, Q = 8N, θ = 60°

**Step 1: Find Magnitude R**

$$R = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ\cos\theta}$$

$$R = \sqrt{(6)^2 + (8)^2 + 2(6)(8)\cos 60°}$$

$$R = \sqrt{36 + 64 + 96 \times \frac{1}{2}}$$

$$R = \sqrt{36 + 64 + 48}$$

$$R = \sqrt{148} = \boxed{2\sqrt{37} \approx 12.2 \text{ N}}$$

---

**Step 2: Find Direction α (angle with P)**

$$\tan\alpha = \frac{Q\sin\theta}{P + Q\cos\theta}$$

$$\tan\alpha = \frac{8 \times \sin 60°}{6 + 8 \times \cos 60°}$$

$$\tan\alpha = \frac{8 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{6 + 8 \times \frac{1}{2}} = \frac{4\sqrt{3}}{6 + 4} = \frac{4\sqrt{3}}{10}$$

$$\tan\alpha = \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{5} \approx 0.693$$

$$\boxed{\alpha \approx 34.7° \text{ with vector P}}$$

---

## 📌 Quick Revision Box

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cosθ)                     │
│  tan α = B sinθ / (A + B cosθ)                  │
│                                                  │
│  θ=0°   → R = A+B  (max)                        │
│  θ=90°  → R = √(A²+B²)                          │
│  θ=180° → R = |A-B| (min)                       │
│  Equal vectors: R = 2A cos(θ/2)                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

> 🏆 **NEET Tip:** At least **1-2 questions** appear every year from vectors. Master the special cases (θ = 0°, 90°, 180°) and the max-min resultant concept — they are the most frequently tested!

## 1. CORE CONCEPT & DEFINITION

### What is an Infinite Plane Sheet?
An **infinite plane sheet** is a theoretical construct of matter extended infinitely in two dimensions with negligible thickness, carrying uniform charge distribution.

### Key Understanding:
- **Uniform surface charge density (σ)**: Charge per unit area = Q/A (measured in C/m²)
- The field is **independent of distance** from the sheet (unlike point charges where E ∝ 1/r²)
- This is a **major conceptual difference** from point charges

### Why Independent of Distance?

Imagine standing closer to an infinite plane:
- You get closer to your point charges ✓ (E increases)
- BUT more charge enters your "field of view" ✗ (which decreases E)
- **These two effects exactly cancel out** → **E remains constant!**

---

## 2. KEY FORMULAS & FACTS

### **Main Formula:**
$$\boxed{E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}}$$

Where:
- **σ** = surface charge density (C/m²)
- **ε₀** = permittivity of free space = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²/N·m²
- **E** = electric field strength (N/C)

### **Important Points:**

| Feature | Details |
|---------|---------|
| **Direction** | Perpendicular to the plane, pointing AWAY if +ve, TOWARDS if -ve |
| **Dependence** | Independent of distance (r) |
| **Field Nature** | Uniform field (constant magnitude & direction) |
| **Superposition** | Two opposite sheets → field only between them |

### **Derivation using Gauss's Law** (Essential for NEET):

**Using Gaussian Surface: Cylindrical Pillbox**

```
         ↑ E
    |---------|  ← Top cap (Area A)
    |         |
    |========| ← Charged Sheet (σ)
    |         |
    |---------|  ← Bottom cap (Area A)
         ↓ E
```

**Applying Gauss's Law:**
$$\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{Q_{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}$$

**Step-by-step:**
1. **Flux through curved surface** = 0 (E ⊥ surface)
2. **Flux through two caps** = E·A + E·A = 2EA
3. **Enclosed charge** = σ·A
4. **Therefore:** $2EA = \frac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0}$
5. **Solving:** $E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ ✓

---

## 3. COMMON NEET QUESTION PATTERNS

### **Pattern 1: Direct Field Calculation**
*"A uniformly charged infinite plane has surface charge density σ = 2 × 10⁻⁸ C/m². Find the electric field at a distance 10 cm from it."*
- **Key Point:** Distance is IRRELEVANT
- **Solution:** Use $E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ directly

### **Pattern 2: Two Parallel Sheets**
- **Same sign charges:** Fields cancel between sheets, add outside
- **Opposite sign charges:** Fields add between sheets, cancel outside
- **Most asked configuration**

### **Pattern 3: Force on a Charged Particle**
- Force between plane and point charge
- Use F = qE

### **Pattern 4: Potential Difference**
- Integrate E over distance: $V = \int E \, dr$
- For infinite plane: $V = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} \cdot d$ (for distance d)

### **Pattern 5: Comparison Questions**
- Compare field from infinite plane vs. point charge at same distance
- Compare two sheets with different σ values

---

## 4. MEMORY TIPS & ANALOGIES

### **Tip 1: The "∞" Asymmetry**
$$\text{Point charge: } E \propto \frac{1}{r^2} \quad \text{vs} \quad \text{Infinite plane: } E = \text{constant}$$

Remember: As you move away, charges appearing in "new area" exactly compensates for distance effect.

### **Tip 2: Factor of 2**
The factor **2** in denominator comes from **two caps** of the Gaussian pillbox getting flux. A single cap would give $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$.

### **Tip 3: Visual Mnemonic**

```
Infinite Plane (like an infinite wall of charges)
↓
Symmetry from both sides
↓
Constant field perpendicular to surface
↓
E = σ/(2ε₀)  [NOT dependent on r]
```

### **Tip 4: Superposition Rule**
| Configuration | Field Between | Field Outside |
|---|---|---|
| **++** (same) | 0 | σ/ε₀ |
| **+-** (opposite) | σ/ε₀ | 0 |

---

## 5. WORKED EXAMPLE (NEET Level)

### **Problem:**
Two infinite parallel planes with uniform surface charge densities +σ and -σ are separated by distance d. A charge q is placed between them at a distance x from the positive plate. Find the force on the charge.

**Solution:**

**Step 1: Identify the field from each sheet**
- Field from +σ sheet: $E_+ = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ (pointing away from it)
- Field from -σ sheet: $E_- = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ (pointing toward it)

**Step 2: Determine field directions (for point between sheets)**
```
    +σ                  -σ
    ||  →E₊→  →E₋→     ||
    ||          (point) ||
```
Both fields point in same direction (from + to -)

**Step 3: Find net field using superposition**
$$E_{net} = E_+ + E_- = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} + \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$$

**Step 4: Calculate force**
$$F = qE_{net} = \frac{q\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$$

**Key Insight:** Position (x) doesn't matter! The field between opposite sheets is uniform.

**Answer Direction:**
- If q is **positive**: Force toward -σ plate
- If q is **negative**: Force toward +σ plate

---

## QUICK CHECKLIST FOR NEET EXAM

✅ **Must Know:**
- [ ] Formula: E = σ/(2ε₀)
- [ ] Field is **perpendicular** to plane
- [ ] Field is **independent of distance**
- [ ] Derive using Gauss's law with pillbox
- [ ] Two sheet superposition rules

✅ **Common Traps:**
- ✗ Don't use E = kq/r² for infinite sheets
- ✗ Don't forget the factor of 2
- ✗ Don't assume field depends on distance
- ✗ Don't mix up superposition of opposite vs same charges

---

## FINAL PRACTICE QUESTIONS

1. **Easy:** Find E for σ = 10⁻⁷ C/m² at distance 5m
2. **Medium:** Two sheets with σ₁ = 2×10⁻⁸ and σ₂ = 3×10⁻⁸ C/m² face each other. Find field between them.
3. **Hard:** A charged particle oscillates between two opposite infinite sheets. Find period of oscillation.

# Relative Velocity in Two Dimensions
### Class 11 | Chapter 4: Motion in a Plane | NEET Physics

---

## 1. 🎯 Core Concept & Definition

**Relative velocity** is the velocity of one object *as observed by another moving object*.

> In simple terms: **"How fast does object A appear to move, when you are sitting on object B?"**

### In One Dimension (Quick Recap):
If two cars move along the same road:
- **Same direction:** V_rel = V_A − V_B
- **Opposite direction:** V_rel = V_A + V_B

### In Two Dimensions (The Real Concept):
When objects move in a **plane** (not just along a line), their velocities are **vectors** — they have both magnitude AND direction.

**The formula becomes:**

$$\vec{V}_{AB} = \vec{V}_A - \vec{V}_B$$

Where:
- $\vec{V}_{AB}$ = velocity of A **with respect to** B
- $\vec{V}_A$ = velocity of A with respect to **ground**
- $\vec{V}_B$ = velocity of B with respect to **ground**

> ⚠️ **Critical point:** You must do **vector subtraction**, NOT simply subtract magnitudes!

---

## 2. 📐 Key Formulas & Important Facts

### Formula 1 — Magnitude of Relative Velocity:
When two objects move at angle **θ** between their velocity vectors:

$$|\vec{V}_{AB}| = \sqrt{V_A^2 + V_B^2 - 2V_AV_B\cos\theta}$$

> This comes directly from the **law of cosines** in vector subtraction

### Formula 2 — Direction of Relative Velocity:
$$\tan\alpha = \frac{V_B \sin\theta}{V_A - V_B \cos\theta}$$

Where **α** is angle of $\vec{V}_{AB}$ with direction of $\vec{V}_A$

### Special Cases Table:

| Angle θ Between Vectors | Relative Speed |
|------------------------|----------------|
| θ = 0° (same direction) | \|V_A − V_B\| → **minimum** |
| θ = 180° (opposite) | V_A + V_B → **maximum** |
| θ = 90° | √(V_A² + V_B²) |
| V_A = V_B, θ = 60° | V (equals individual speed) |

### 🌧️ Rain-Man Problem (Most Common in NEET):

If rain falls vertically with velocity **$\vec{V}_r$** and man walks horizontally with velocity **$\vec{V}_m$**:

$$\vec{V}_{rain\,w.r.t.\,man} = \vec{V}_{rain} - \vec{V}_{man}$$

**To avoid getting wet → hold umbrella in the direction of relative velocity of rain**

$$\tan\theta = \frac{V_m}{V_r}$$
*(angle from vertical, tilted forward)*

---

## 3. 📝 Common NEET Question Patterns

### Pattern 1: 🌧️ Rain-Man Problem
*"Rain falls vertically. Man walks east. At what angle should he hold his umbrella?"*
→ Use vector subtraction, find angle with vertical

### Pattern 2: 🚢 River-Boat Problem
*"Boat heads perpendicular to river current. Find actual velocity/direction"*
→ Resultant of boat velocity + river velocity
→ Drift = river speed × crossing time

### Pattern 3: ✈️ Airplane + Wind
*"Plane flies north at 500 km/h, wind blows east at 100 km/h. Find resultant velocity"*
→ Vector addition of plane + wind velocities

### Pattern 4: 🚗 Two Moving Vehicles
*"Two cars approach each other / move at an angle. Find relative velocity"*
→ Direct application of $\vec{V}_{AB} = \vec{V}_A - \vec{V}_B$

### Pattern 5: 🏊 Swimmer crossing river
*"Swimmer wants to reach directly opposite bank. Find required angle of swimming"*
→ Condition: horizontal component of swim velocity = river current

---

## 4. 🧠 Memory Tips & Analogies

### Analogy 1 — The Train Window:
> Sit inside a moving train and look at a tree. The tree appears to move **backward**. That's relative velocity — the tree's velocity relative to you = 0 − V_train = **−V_train** (backward direction) ✓

### Analogy 2 — The Rain Trick:
> When you're stationary, rain hits you from **above** (vertical).
> When you **run forward**, rain appears to hit you from the **front** (tilted).
> The faster you run → more the tilt → hold umbrella more forward!

### Memory Formula Trick:
$$\vec{V}_{AB} = \vec{V}_A - \vec{V}_B$$
**"A with respect to B = A minus B"**
→ Read it as: **"A minus B"** — same order as the subscript AB 🎯

### For the Magnitude Formula:
Remember it as the **cosine rule** of a triangle:
> Draw $\vec{V}_A$ and **$-\vec{V}_B$** (reversed $\vec{V}_B$) as two sides → the resultant is $\vec{V}_{AB}$

---

## 5. ✏️ Example Problem with Solution

### Problem:
> Rain is falling vertically with a speed of **10 m/s**. A woman rides a bicycle with a speed of **10 m/s** in the East direction. What is the direction in which she should hold her umbrella?

---

### Solution:

**Step 1: Identify the velocities**
- $\vec{V}_{rain}$ = 10 m/s (vertically downward) → let's say **−ĵ** direction
- $\vec{V}_{woman}$ = 10 m/s (East) → **+î** direction

**Step 2: Apply the formula**
$$\vec{V}_{rain\,w.r.t.\,woman} = \vec{V}_{rain} - \vec{V}_{woman}$$

$$= (-10\hat{j}) - (10\hat{i})$$

$$= -10\hat{i} - 10\hat{j}$$

**Step 3: Find the magnitude**
$$|\vec{V}_{rel}| = \sqrt{(-10)^2 + (-10)^2} = \sqrt{200} = 10\sqrt{2} \text{ m/s}$$

**Step 4: Find the direction**
$$\tan\theta = \frac{V_{horizontal}}{V_{vertical}} = \frac{10}{10} = 1$$

$$\theta = 45°$$

**Step 5: Interpret the answer**
The relative velocity of rain is directed at **45° from vertical, towards West** (since woman moves East, rain appears to come from front-East side).

**∴ She should hold her umbrella at 45° from vertical, tilted towards the East (forward direction)**

---

### 📊 Vector Diagram:

```
        ↑ (against motion, West)
        |  \
        |    \  ← V_rain w.r.t. woman
        |  45° \
        |________\
     (Vertical,    (Horizontal,
      downward)     Westward)
```

---

## 🔑 Quick Revision Box

| Key Point | Remember |
|-----------|----------|
| Formula | $\vec{V}_{AB} = \vec{V}_A - \vec{V}_B$ |
| Magnitude | $\sqrt{V_A^2 + V_B^2 - 2V_AV_B\cos\theta}$ |
| Rain-umbrella angle | $\tan\theta = V_{man}/V_{rain}$ from vertical |
| Max relative speed | When moving opposite (θ=180°) |
| Min relative speed | When moving same direction (θ=0°) |
| Vector or scalar? | Always **VECTOR** — direction matters! |

---

> 💡 **NEET Exam Tip:** In rain-man problems, always draw a vector diagram first. Most mistakes happen when students add instead of subtract velocities. Remember: **relative velocity = subtraction of velocity vectors**, then find magnitude using Pythagoras or cosine rule! 🎯

# Multiplication of Vectors by Real Numbers
### Class 11 | Chapter 4: Motion in a Plane | NEET Physics

---

## 1. 🧠 Core Concept and Definition

When a vector **A** is multiplied by a **real number (scalar) λ**, the result is a **new vector** whose:
- **Magnitude** = |λ| × |**A**|
- **Direction** depends on the **sign of λ**

> Think of it as "scaling" a vector — you're stretching or shrinking it, and possibly flipping its direction.

### Three Cases:

| Value of λ | Magnitude of new vector | Direction |
|------------|------------------------|-----------|
| λ > 0 (positive) | λ × \|**A**\| (larger/smaller) | **Same** as **A** |
| λ < 0 (negative) | \|λ\| × \|**A**\| | **Opposite** to **A** |
| λ = 0 | 0 | **Null vector** |

### Special Sub-cases:
- If λ = **+1** → vector remains **unchanged**
- If λ = **−1** → vector has **same magnitude, opposite direction** (this is the **negative of a vector**)
- If λ = **2** → vector **doubles** in magnitude, same direction
- If λ = **½** → vector **halves** in magnitude, same direction

---

## 2. 📐 Key Formulas & Important Facts

### Basic Formula:
$$\vec{B} = \lambda\vec{A}$$
$$|\vec{B}| = |\lambda| \cdot |\vec{A}|$$

### Distributive Laws:
$$\lambda(\vec{A} + \vec{B}) = \lambda\vec{A} + \lambda\vec{B}$$
$$(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)\vec{A} = \lambda_1\vec{A} + \lambda_2\vec{A}$$

### Associative Law:
$$\lambda_1(\lambda_2\vec{A}) = (\lambda_1\lambda_2)\vec{A}$$

### Unit Vector Formula (most important for NEET!):
$$\hat{A} = \frac{\vec{A}}{|\vec{A}|}$$

> Here, we multiply vector **A** by the scalar $\frac{1}{|\vec{A}|}$ to get a **unit vector** in the direction of **A**. This is the most powerful application of scalar multiplication!

### Key Physical Examples:
| Physics Concept | Scalar × Vector |
|----------------|-----------------|
| Force = mass × acceleration | F = m**a** (m is scalar) |
| Momentum = mass × velocity | **p** = m**v** |
| Displacement = speed × time (direction matters) | involves scalar multiplication |
| Weight = mg (downward) | **W** = m**g** |

---

## 3. 🎯 Common NEET Question Patterns

### Pattern 1: Finding unit vector
*"Find the unit vector in the direction of **A** = 3î + 4ĵ"*

### Pattern 2: Negative of a vector
*"If **F** = 5î − 3ĵ N, what is −**F**?"*

### Pattern 3: Identifying direction after multiplication
*"A vector **v** points East. What is the direction of −3**v**?"*

### Pattern 4: Physical application
*"A force **F** acts on a body. What force acts in the opposite direction with double magnitude?"*
→ Answer: −2**F**

### Pattern 5: Algebra of vectors
*"If **A** = 2î + 3ĵ, find 3**A** − 2**A**"*

---

## 4. 💡 Memory Tip / Analogy

### 🎸 "Volume Knob" Analogy:
Think of a vector like **sound coming from a speaker in one direction.**

- Turning the volume **UP** (+ve scalar > 1) → louder sound, **same direction**
- Turning it **DOWN** (+ve scalar < 1) → softer sound, **same direction**
- Pressing **MUTE** (scalar = 0) → no sound = null vector
- **Reversing the speaker** (−ve scalar) → same intensity sound, but coming from **opposite direction**

### 🔑 Quick Memory Rule:
> **"Sign decides direction, magnitude decides size"**
> - **Positive scalar** → Same direction ✅
> - **Negative scalar** → Flip direction 🔄

---

## 5. 📝 Example Problem with Solution

### Problem:
A vector **A** = 4î + 3ĵ m.
**(a)** Find the magnitude of **A**
**(b)** Find the unit vector $\hat{A}$
**(c)** Find a vector **B** that has **magnitude 10 m** in the **same direction** as **A**

---

### Solution:

**Step 1: Find magnitude of A**
$$|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{(4)^2 + (3)^2} = \sqrt{16 + 9} = \sqrt{25} = 5 \text{ m}$$

---

**Step 2: Find unit vector $\hat{A}$**

Using the formula: $\hat{A} = \dfrac{\vec{A}}{|\vec{A}|}$

$$\hat{A} = \frac{4\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}}{5} = \frac{4}{5}\hat{i} + \frac{3}{5}\hat{j}$$

$$\hat{A} = 0.8\hat{i} + 0.6\hat{j}$$

✅ **Verify:** $|\hat{A}| = \sqrt{(0.8)^2 + (0.6)^2} = \sqrt{0.64 + 0.36} = \sqrt{1} = 1$ ✔️

---

**Step 3: Find vector B with magnitude 10 m in same direction**

We need to **multiply** the unit vector $\hat{A}$ by scalar **10**:

$$\vec{B} = 10 \times \hat{A} = 10 \times \left(\frac{4}{5}\hat{i} + \frac{3}{5}\hat{j}\right)$$

$$\boxed{\vec{B} = 8\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} \text{ m}}$$

**Verify:** $|\vec{B}| = \sqrt{64 + 36} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ m ✔️

---

## 🏆 NEET Exam Quick Recap

| Key Point | Remember This |
|-----------|---------------|
| Unit vector formula | $\hat{A} = \vec{A}/\|\vec{A}\|$ |
| Negative vector | Same magnitude, opposite direction |
| Null vector | Any vector × 0 |
| Physical application | F = ma, p = mv use this concept |
| Distributive law | λ(A+B) = λA + λB |

> **NEET Tip:** Unit vector problems appear almost every year — master Step 2 above and you'll never lose those marks! 🎯

# 📐 Resolution of Vectors
### Class 11 | Chapter 4: Motion in a Plane | NEET Physics

---

## 1. 🧠 Core Concept & Definition

**Resolution of a vector** is the process of **splitting a single vector into two or more component vectors** that together produce the same effect as the original vector.

> Think of it as the **reverse of vector addition** — instead of combining vectors, we're breaking one apart.

### Why Do We Do This?
Nature doesn't always cooperate with our coordinate axes. A ball thrown at an angle, a force applied diagonally — these need to be **broken into manageable horizontal and vertical parts** so we can apply equations of motion separately in each direction.

### The Fundamental Idea:
A vector **→A** in a plane can be resolved into:
- A component along the **X-axis** (horizontal)
- A component along the **Y-axis** (vertical)

These two components are called **rectangular components** (because they are at 90° to each other).

```
          Y
          |        → A (original vector)
          |       /
      Ay  |      /
          |     /  θ
          |____/_________ X
              Ax
```

---

## 2. 📌 Key Formulas & Important Facts

### ✅ Rectangular Components of a Vector

If vector **→A** makes angle **θ** with the positive X-axis:

$$\boxed{A_x = A\cos\theta}$$

$$\boxed{A_y = A\sin\theta}$$

Where:
- **A** = magnitude of the original vector
- **Aₓ** = horizontal component (along X-axis)
- **Aᵧ** = vertical component (along Y-axis)

---

### ✅ Recovering the Original Vector from Components

| Property | Formula |
|----------|---------|
| **Magnitude** | $A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$ |
| **Direction (angle)** | $\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{A_y}{A_x}\right)$ |

> **NEET Key Point:** These two formulas are used in the **reverse direction** — given components, find the resultant.

---

### ✅ Component Form Using Unit Vectors

$$\boxed{\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j}}$$

- **î** = unit vector along X-axis
- **ĵ** = unit vector along Y-axis
- In 3D: **→A** = Aₓî + Aᵧĵ + A_z k̂

---

### ✅ Key Properties to Remember

| Condition | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|
| θ = 0° | Aₓ = A (max), Aᵧ = 0 |
| θ = 90° | Aₓ = 0, Aᵧ = A (max) |
| θ = 45° | Aₓ = Aᵧ = A/√2 |
| θ = 30° | Aₓ = A√3/2, Aᵧ = A/2 |
| θ = 60° | Aₓ = A/2, Aᵧ = A√3/2 |

> 🔺 **Quick Trick:** cos → the angle side, sin → the opposite side
> In a right triangle, cos is "close" to the angle, sin is "separated" from it.

---

### ✅ Rectangular Components Along ANY Two Perpendicular Directions

The axes don't have to be horizontal/vertical. If two **perpendicular directions** are chosen:
- Component along one direction = **A cosθ**
- Component along the other = **A sinθ**

This is used heavily in **inclined plane problems!**

---

## 3. 🎯 Common NEET Question Patterns

### Pattern 1: Direct Component Calculation
> *"A force of 20N acts at 60° to the horizontal. Find its horizontal and vertical components."*

**→ Apply Aₓ = Acosθ, Aᵧ = Asinθ directly**

---

### Pattern 2: Resultant from Components
> *"Two forces 3N along X-axis and 4N along Y-axis act on a body. Find the resultant."*

**→ Use R = √(3² + 4²) = 5N, θ = tan⁻¹(4/3)**

---

### Pattern 3: Inclined Plane (Most Frequent!)
> *"A block on an inclined plane at angle θ. Resolve weight mg."*

```
         /|
        / |
       /  |
      /θ  |
     /____| 

Along the plane: mg sinθ (pulls block down the slope)
Perpendicular to plane: mg cosθ (into the surface = Normal force)
```

**→ Weight mg is resolved as:**
- **Parallel to incline** = mg sinθ *(causes sliding)*
- **Perpendicular to incline** = mg cosθ *(balanced by normal force N)*

> ⚠️ **Most common NEET trap:** Students swap sinθ and cosθ here. Remember: **sinθ is along the slope** (sliding component).

---

### Pattern 4: Projectile Motion (Uses Resolution Concept)
> *"A ball is projected at 30° with velocity 20 m/s. Find horizontal and vertical components."*

- uₓ = u cosθ = 20 cos30° = 20 × (√3/2) = 10√3 m/s
- uᵧ = u sinθ = 20 sin30° = 20 × (1/2) = 10 m/s

**→ These components are then used separately in equations of motion**

---

### Pattern 5: Equilibrium of Forces
> *"Three forces act on a particle in equilibrium. Find the unknown force."*

**→ Sum of all X-components = 0 AND Sum of all Y-components = 0**

$$\sum F_x = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \sum F_y = 0$$

---

## 4. 💡 Memory Tips & Analogies

### 🏠 The "Ramp Analogy"
Imagine pushing a heavy sofa up a ramp:
- Part of your force goes **along the ramp** (useful work) → **sin component**
- Part goes **into the ramp** (wasted, balanced by normal force) → **cos component**

---

### 🧭 The "GPS Analogy"
A GPS might say "travel 10 km at 30° North of East."
- You can think of this as: **8.66 km East + 5 km North**
- That's exactly resolution — one diagonal instruction → two straight instructions!

---

### 📝 SOH-CAH-TOA Reminder

```
         |Opposite

         |Hypotenuse

         |Adjacent

         |Hypotenuse
```

> **Pro Tip:** In vector resolution, the **hypotenuse is always the original vector**. The components are always the **two shorter sides.**

---

### 🎯 The "Always Cosθ with the Angle" Rule
- The component **in the direction of θ** → **multiply by cosθ**
- The component **perpendicular to θ** → **multiply by sinθ**

---

### Question:
> A vector of magnitude **10 units** makes an angle of **30°** with the positive X-axis. Another vector of magnitude **10 units** makes an angle of **120°** with the positive X-axis. Find the **magnitude and direction of their resultant**.

### Solution:

---

# Uniform Circular Motion (UCM)
### Class 11 | Chapter 4: Motion in a Plane | NEET Physics

---

## 1. 🎯 Core Concept & Definition

**Uniform Circular Motion** is the motion of an object moving along a **circular path** with **constant speed**.

> ⚠️ KEY DISTINCTION — Speed is constant, but **velocity is NOT constant** because the **direction** of motion keeps changing at every point.

### What this means physically:
| Quantity | Status in UCM |
|----------|--------------|
| Speed | ✅ Constant |
| Velocity | ❌ Changing (direction changes) |
| Acceleration | ✅ Exists (due to change in velocity direction) |
| Kinetic Energy | ✅ Constant |
| Momentum | ❌ Changing |

### Direction of Key Vectors:
```
        v (tangential)
        ↑
        |
← a ────●──────→ Circle
(centripetal,    
towards center)
```

- **Velocity (v)** → Always **tangential** to the circle (perpendicular to radius)
- **Centripetal Acceleration (a)** → Always **towards the center** (centripetal = "center-seeking")
- **v and a are always perpendicular** → That's why speed doesn't change!

---

## 2. 📐 Key Formulas

### Angular Velocity (ω)
$$\boxed{\omega = \frac{\theta}{t} = \frac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi f}$$

- Unit: **rad/s**
- ω tells how fast the angle sweeps

---

### Relationship Between Linear & Angular Velocity
$$\boxed{v = r\omega}$$

- v = linear/tangential speed (m/s)
- r = radius of circular path (m)

---

### Centripetal Acceleration
$$\boxed{a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r = \frac{4\pi^2 r}{T^2}}$$

- Direction: **Always towards the center**
- This is a **real acceleration** (causes direction change)

---

### Centripetal Force
$$\boxed{F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r}$$

- **NOT a new force** — it is the **net force directed towards center**
- It can be provided by: Tension, Gravity, Normal force, Friction, etc.

---

### Time Period & Frequency
$$\boxed{T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}} \quad \text{and} \quad \boxed{f = \frac{1}{T}}$$

---

### 🔴 Centrifugal Force (Pseudo Force)
- Only observed in **rotating (non-inertial) frame**
- Equal in magnitude but **opposite in direction** to centripetal force
- **Does NOT exist** in ground (inertial) frame

---

## 3. 🧠 Common NEET Question Patterns

### Pattern 1: Finding centripetal acceleration/force
> "A particle moves in a circle of radius 2m with speed 4 m/s. Find centripetal acceleration."
→ Direct formula: $a = v²/r$

---

### Pattern 2: Angle between velocity and acceleration
> "What is the angle between velocity and acceleration in UCM?"
→ **Always 90°** (they are perpendicular)

---

### Pattern 3: Change in velocity over half/quarter revolution
> "A particle completes half revolution. Find change in velocity."

- After half revolution: velocity reverses direction
$$|\Delta v| = |v_f - v_i| = v - (-v) = 2v$$

- After quarter revolution: directions are perpendicular
$$|\Delta v| = \sqrt{v^2 + v^2} = v\sqrt{2}$$

---

### Pattern 4: Work done by centripetal force
> "How much work is done by centripetal force?"
→ **Work = 0** always! (Force ⊥ displacement, cos90° = 0)

---

### Pattern 5: Comparing quantities when r or v changes
> "If speed doubles with same radius, centripetal force becomes?"
→ $F_c \propto v^2$, so F becomes **4 times**

---

## 4. 💡 Memory Tip & Analogy

### 🌀 The Stone-in-a-Sling Analogy:
Imagine swinging a stone tied to a string in a circle:
- Your **hand pulling the string** = Centripetal force (towards center)
- The stone always tries to **fly away tangentially** (Newton's 1st law)
- The moment you release → stone flies off **tangentially** (not outward!)

### 🧠 Memory Tricks:

| Formula | Trick |
|---------|-------|
| $v = rω$ | **"Very Relaxed ω"** → v, r, ω |
| $a = v²/r$ | **"A Very²/Rough road"** |
| Work by F_c = 0 | **Force ⊥ velocity → Zero work** |
| ω = 2πf | **"omega equals 2π × frequency"** → think of full circle (2π) per second |

---

## 5. 📝 Example Problem (NEET-Style)

**Question:**
A particle of mass 0.1 kg is moving in a circular path of radius 1 m. If its angular velocity is 2π rad/s, find:
(a) Linear speed
(b) Centripetal acceleration
(c) Centripetal force

---

**Solution:**

**Given:**
- m = 0.1 kg
- r = 1 m
- ω = 2π rad/s

---

**(a) Linear Speed:**
$$v = r\omega = 1 \times 2\pi = 2\pi \approx 6.28 \text{ m/s}$$

---

**(b) Centripetal Acceleration:**
$$a_c = \omega^2 r = (2\pi)^2 \times 1 = 4\pi^2 \approx 39.5 \text{ m/s}^2$$

---

**(c) Centripetal Force:**
$$F_c = ma_c = 0.1 \times 4\pi^2 = 0.4\pi^2 \approx 3.95 \text{ N}$$

*Direction: Towards the center of the circle*

---

## 🔑 Quick Revision Box

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         UCM — MUST REMEMBER FOR NEET        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ✅ Speed = constant; Velocity = variable    │
│ ✅ v ⊥ a (always 90° between them)         │
│ ✅ v = rω | a = v²/r | F = mv²/r           │
│ ✅ Work by centripetal force = ZERO         │
│ ✅ Centrifugal force = pseudo force only    │
│ ✅ Release → object moves TANGENTIALLY      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

> 📌 **NEET Tip:** Every year, 1–2 questions appear from UCM. Focus on: centripetal force calculations, change in velocity vectors, and work done. These are the highest-yield sub-topics!

# Resolution of Vectors — Class 11, Chapter 4
## Complete NEET Guide

---

## 1. 🎯 Core Concept & Definition

**Resolution of a vector** is the process of splitting a single vector into **two or more component vectors** that together produce the **same effect** as the original vector.

> Think of it as the **reverse of vector addition** — instead of combining vectors, you break one vector into parts.

### Why Do We Resolve Vectors?
> Because **mathematics is easier along straight lines (axes)** than at angles!

---

### 📐 Resolution in a Plane (2D)

Consider a vector **A** making angle **θ** with the positive X-axis:

```
Y
↑
|   /→ A (resultant)
|  /
| / θ
|/________→ X
```

The vector **A** is resolved into:
- **Horizontal Component (Aₓ)** → along X-axis
- **Vertical Component (Aᵧ)** → along Y-axis

These components are **mutually perpendicular** (at 90° to each other).

---

## 2. 🔑 Key Formulas

### Primary Resolution Formulas:

| Component | Formula | Direction |
|-----------|---------|-----------|
| X-component | **Aₓ = A cos θ** | Along X-axis |
| Y-component | **Aᵧ = A sin θ** | Along Y-axis |

Where:
- **A** = magnitude of original vector
- **θ** = angle with positive X-axis

### In Unit Vector Notation:
$$\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j}$$
$$\vec{A} = A\cos\theta\,\hat{i} + A\sin\theta\,\hat{j}$$

---

### Reverse Process — Reconstructing from Components:

| Quantity | Formula |
|----------|---------|
| **Magnitude** | $A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$ |
| **Direction** | $\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{A_y}{A_x}\right)$ |

---

### ⚡ Important Angle Table (Memorize!):

| θ | cos θ (→ Aₓ) | sin θ (↑ Aᵧ) |
|---|--------------|--------------|
| 0° | 1 | 0 |
| 30° | √3/2 | 1/2 |
| 45° | 1/√2 | 1/√2 |
| 60° | 1/2 | √3/2 |
| 90° | 0 | 1 |

---

### Resolution in 3D:
$$\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j} + A_z\hat{k}$$
$$A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2}$$

---

## 3. 📋 Common NEET Question Patterns

### Pattern 1: Direct Component Finding
> *"A force of 20 N acts at 60° to the horizontal. Find its horizontal and vertical components."*
- Straightforward: use Aₓ = A cos θ, Aᵧ = A sin θ

---

### Pattern 2: Vector Addition Using Resolution
> *"Two vectors of magnitude 3 and 4 act at 90° to each other. Find the resultant."*
- Resolve each → add components → reconstruct magnitude

---

### Pattern 3: Inclined Plane (Most Common in NEET! ⭐)
> *"A block on a 30° incline... find component of weight along and perpendicular to surface."*

```
       /|
      / |
     /  | mg (downward)
    /θ  |
   /    |
  /_____|
```

- **Along incline** (causes sliding) = **mg sin θ**
- **Perpendicular to incline** (causes normal force) = **mg cos θ**

> 🔴 **NEET Trap:** Many students confuse which is sin and which is cos on inclined planes!
> **Rule:** The component *opposing the steeper direction* uses **sin θ**

---

### Pattern 4: Projectile Motion
> The entire concept of projectile motion is based on resolution!
- **Horizontal:** uₓ = u cos θ (constant, no acceleration)
- **Vertical:** uᵧ = u sin θ (affected by gravity)

---

### Pattern 5: Equilibrium Problems
> *"Three concurrent forces are in equilibrium. Find the unknown force."*
- Sum of X-components = 0
- Sum of Y-components = 0

---

## 4. 💡 Memory Tips & Analogies

### 🎭 The "Shadow Analogy":
> Imagine shining a **torch horizontally** on a vector arrow — the **shadow on the wall = vertical component (sin θ)**. Shine the torch **vertically** — the **shadow on the floor = horizontal component (cos θ)**.

---

### 🎵 The Golden Rule to Never Forget:
> **"cos θ goes with the CLOSER axis"**
> If θ is measured from X-axis → X-component uses **cos θ**
> If θ is measured from Y-axis → Y-component uses **cos θ**

---

### 🧠 NEET Shortcut for Inclined Planes:
> Draw the incline. The weight mg goes straight down.
> **"The angle at TOP of the triangle = same as incline angle θ"**
> - mg **sin θ** → **parallel** to slope (along the surface)
> - mg **cos θ** → **perpendicular** to slope (into the surface)

---

## 5. ✏️ Example Problem (NEET Style)

### Problem:
> A vector **F** = 10 N acts at an angle of 30° above the negative X-axis (in the second quadrant). Find its X and Y components and write it in unit vector notation.

---

### Solution:

**Step 1: Identify the angle properly**

The vector is in the **2nd quadrant**, making 30° with the negative X-axis.
∴ Angle from positive X-axis = **180° - 30° = 150°**

---

**Step 2: Apply resolution formulas**

$$F_x = F\cos 150° = 10 \times \left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = -5\sqrt{3} \text{ N}$$

$$F_y = F\sin 150° = 10 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = +5 \text{ N}$$

---

**Step 3: Unit vector notation**

$$\boxed{\vec{F} = -5\sqrt{3}\,\hat{i} + 5\,\hat{j} \text{ N}}$$

---

**Step 4: Verify magnitude**

$$F = \sqrt{(-5\sqrt{3})^2 + (5)^2} = \sqrt{75 + 25} = \sqrt{100} = 10 \text{ N ✓}$$

---

**Step 5: Verify direction**

$$\tan\alpha = \frac{|F_y|}{|F_x|} = \frac{5}{5\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \Rightarrow \alpha = 30° \text{ from negative X-axis ✓}$$

---

## 🔴 NEET Common Mistakes to Avoid:

| ❌ Mistake | ✅ Correct Approach |
|-----------|-------------------|
| Using sin for horizontal when angle is from X-axis | Horizontal = **cos θ** when θ from X-axis |
| Forgetting negative signs in 2nd/3rd quadrant | Always check which quadrant! |
| Confusing incline components | Along slope = mg **sin θ**, Normal = mg **cos θ** |
| Not verifying with magnitude formula | Always check: √(Aₓ² + Aᵧ²) = A |

```
# Equality of Vectors — Class 11, Chapter 4 | NEET Physics

---

## 1. 🧠 Core Concept & Definition

> **Two vectors are said to be equal if and only if they have the SAME magnitude AND the SAME direction.**

This seems simple, but students often confuse it — **both conditions must be satisfied simultaneously.**

### What Makes Two Vectors Equal?

| Condition | Requirement |
|-----------|-------------|
| Magnitude | Must be **identical** (same numerical value + same unit) |
| Direction | Must be **exactly the same** (same angle, same sense) |

### Critical Point — Position Does NOT Matter!
A vector is a **free vector** — it can be translated (shifted) anywhere in space **without changing its value**, as long as magnitude and direction are preserved.

```
→A = ———→         →B = ———→ (shifted to another location)
     
Both are EQUAL because same length, same direction
```

This means a vector has **no fixed point of application** in the context of equality.

---

## 2. 📐 Key Facts & Mathematical Representation

### Formal Definition:
If **→A = →B**, then:
- |**→A**| = |**→B**| → **(magnitudes are equal)**
- **â = b̂** → **(unit vectors/directions are equal)**

### In Component Form:
Two vectors are equal **if and only if ALL corresponding components are equal:**

$$\vec{A} = \vec{B} \implies A_x = B_x, \quad A_y = B_y, \quad A_z = B_z$$

> This is the **most important and testable** form for NEET!

### What is NOT sufficient for equality:

| Situation | Equal? | Reason |
|-----------|--------|--------|
| Same magnitude, opposite directions | ❌ No | **→A** and **-→A** are NOT equal |
| Same direction, different magnitudes | ❌ No | 5 m/s ≠ 10 m/s even if same direction |
| Same magnitude, perpendicular directions | ❌ No | Direction mismatch |
| Both conditions met, different positions | ✅ Yes | Position is irrelevant |

---

## 3. 🎯 Common NEET Question Patterns

### Pattern 1: Component-based equality
> *"If vector →A = 3î + 4ĵ and →B = aî + bĵ, and →A = →B, find a and b"*

**Approach:** Simply equate components → a = 3, b = 4

---

### Pattern 2: Conceptual trap question
> *"A vector →A is displaced parallel to itself to a new position. The new vector is:"*
> - (a) Different from →A
> - (b) Equal to →A ✅
> - (c) Negative of →A
> - (d) Cannot be determined

**Answer: (b)** — Parallel displacement preserves both magnitude and direction.

---

### Pattern 3: Negative vector confusion
> *"Which of the following vectors is NOT equal to →A = 2î + 3ĵ?"*
> - (a) 2î + 3ĵ (at origin)
> - (b) 2î + 3ĵ (at point P)
> - (c) -2î - 3ĵ ← **This one** ❌
> - (d) 2î + 3ĵ (at point Q)

**Trick:** Option (c) is the **negative** of →A, not equal to it.

---

### Pattern 4: Resultant and equality
> *"→A + →B = →A. What can you say about →B?"*

**Answer:** →B must be a **null/zero vector** (→0)
Because: →A + →0 = →A ✅

---

## 4. 💡 Memory Tip & Analogy

### The "Twin Brothers Analogy":
> Think of two vectors like twin brothers — they are truly "equal" only if they are **identical in every way**: same height (magnitude) AND facing the same direction. Just because they look the same height but face opposite directions doesn't make them equal — that would make one the "negative" of the other!

---

### Quick Memory Formula:
```
EQUAL VECTORS = Same MAGNITUDE + Same DIRECTION
                     (M)              (D)

Forget either M or D → NOT equal!
```

### Also Remember:
- **Equal vectors** → same magnitude, same direction
- **Negative vectors** → same magnitude, **opposite** direction
- **Null vector** → magnitude = 0, direction undefined

---

## 5. ✏️ Example Problem with Solution

### Problem:
> Two vectors are given as:
> **→P** = 5î + 12ĵ and **→Q** = 5î + 12ĵ (but →Q is positioned at point (3, 4))
>
> **(a)** Are →P and →Q equal?
> **(b)** What is |→P| and |→Q|?
> **(c)** If →R = 5î - 12ĵ, is →R equal to →P?

---

### Solution:

**(a) Checking equality of →P and →Q:**

Step 1 — Compare components:
- î components: 5 = 5 ✅
- ĵ components: 12 = 12 ✅

Step 2 — Position check:
- Position does NOT affect vector equality

**∴ →P = →Q ✅ (They ARE equal)**

---

**(b) Finding magnitudes:**

$$|\vec{P}| = \sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{25 + 144} = \sqrt{169} = \boxed{13 \text{ units}}$$

$$|\vec{Q}| = \sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{169} = \boxed{13 \text{ units}}$$

*(As expected — equal vectors have equal magnitudes)*

---

**(c) Is →R = →P?**

- →P = 5î + 12ĵ
- →R = 5î **- 12**ĵ

Step 1 — Compare î: 5 = 5 ✅
Step 2 — Compare ĵ: **12 ≠ -12** ❌

**∴ →P ≠ →R**

In fact, |→R| = 13 (same magnitude), **BUT** direction is different.
→R is obtained by reflecting →P across the x-axis.

> 🔑 Key takeaway: **Same magnitude ALONE is not enough for equality!**

---

## 📦 NEET Revision Box

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         EQUALITY OF VECTORS — NEET FACTS     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ✅ Equal vectors: |A|=|B| AND direction same │
│ ✅ Position/location: DOESN'T matter         │
│ ✅ Component form: Ax=Bx, Ay=By, Az=Bz       │
│ ❌ Same magnitude ≠ necessarily equal        │
│ ❌ Opposite directions = Negative vector     │
│ ❌ Parallel shift changes NOTHING            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

> 💬 **Pro NEET Tip:** Questions on vector equality often appear **embedded inside larger problems** (like relative velocity or projectile motion). Always verify BOTH magnitude and direction before declaring two vectors equal. The most common trap is choosing vectors with equal magnitudes but ignoring direction! 🎯

# 🎯 Projectile Motion — Complete NEET Guide
### Class 11 | Chapter 4: Motion in a Plane

---

## 1. 🧠 Core Concept & Definition

> **A projectile is any object thrown into the air that moves under the influence of gravity alone (no air resistance).**

When you throw a ball at an angle, it follows a **curved path called a trajectory**. This motion has **TWO independent components:**

```
📌 KEY INSIGHT: Horizontal and Vertical motions are COMPLETELY INDEPENDENT of each other
```

| Component | Direction | Acceleration | Type of Motion |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|----------------|
| **Horizontal (x)** | Along ground | **Zero** (no force) | Uniform (constant velocity) |
| **Vertical (y)** | Up/Down | **g = 10 m/s²** (downward) | Uniformly accelerated |

### 🔹 How it's launched:
If a projectile is launched with velocity **u** at angle **θ** with horizontal:

```
        uᵧ = u sinθ (vertical component)
       ↑  ↗
       | /  
       |/ θ
       ────────→ uₓ = u cosθ (horizontal component)
```

- **Horizontal velocity** → `uₓ = u cosθ` *(remains constant throughout)*
- **Vertical velocity** → `uᵧ = u sinθ` *(changes due to gravity)*

---

## 2. 📐 Key Formulas — Master These!

### 🔸 At any time **t**:

| Quantity | Formula | Trick to Remember |
|----------|---------|------------------|
| Horizontal velocity | `vₓ = u cosθ` | Never changes! |
| Vertical velocity | `vᵧ = u sinθ - gt` | Standard v = u - at |
| Horizontal displacement | `x = u cosθ · t` | Simple = speed × time |
| Vertical displacement | `y = u sinθ · t - ½gt²` | Standard s = ut - ½gt² |

---

### 🔸 The Big Four — Most Tested in NEET:

#### ① Time of Flight (T)
$$T = \frac{2u\sinθ}{g}$$
> *Time for projectile to return to same horizontal level*

#### ② Maximum Height (H)
$$H = \frac{u^2\sin^2θ}{2g}$$
> *Highest point reached above launch level*

#### ③ Horizontal Range (R)
$$R = \frac{u^2\sin2θ}{g}$$
> *Horizontal distance covered when it lands*

#### ④ Equation of Trajectory (Shape of path)
$$y = x\tanθ - \frac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2θ}$$
> *This is a **parabola** — confirms the curved path*

---

### 🔸 Special Angle Results (Frequently Tested!):

```
🎯 Maximum Range → θ = 45°     → R_max = u²/g

🎯 Same Range for two angles → θ and (90° - θ)
   Example: 30° and 60° give SAME range!

🎯 At Highest Point:
   • Vertical velocity = 0
   • Horizontal velocity = u cosθ (still present!)
   • Speed is MINIMUM (not zero, unless θ = 90°)
   • KE is MINIMUM, PE is MAXIMUM
```

---

## 3. 📋 Common NEET Question Patterns

### Pattern 1: **"Find the angle for maximum range"**
> Always **θ = 45°** → R = u²/g
> *(Direct 1-mark question)*

---

### Pattern 2: **"Two angles giving same range"**
> If R is same for θ₁ and θ₂, then **θ₁ + θ₂ = 90°**
> *Example: 20° & 70°, 30° & 60°, 25° & 65°*

---

### Pattern 3: **"Velocity/Speed at highest point"**
> At maximum height:
> - **vᵧ = 0** (vertical becomes zero)
> - **vₓ = u cosθ** (horizontal remains)
> - **Speed = u cosθ** (minimum speed during flight)

---

### Pattern 4: **"Ratio of H to R"**
$$\frac{H}{R} = \frac{\tan θ}{4}$$
> Very commonly asked — memorize this derived result!

---

### Pattern 5: **"Projectile from a height / horizontal projection"**
> Ball thrown *horizontally* (θ = 0°):
> - `uₓ = u`, `uᵧ = 0`
> - Time to fall height h: **t = √(2h/g)**
> - Range: **R = u × √(2h/g)**

---

### Pattern 6: **"Comparing KE/PE at different points"**
> At highest point:
> $$KE_{top} = \frac{1}{2}m(u\cosθ)^2 = KE_{initial} \times \cos^2θ$$

---

## 4. 💡 Memory Tips & Analogies

### 🏏 The Cricket Analogy:
> Think of a **cricket ball hit at an angle** — it goes up (vertical component fighting gravity) while moving forward (horizontal component constant). The ball doesn't know about height — it just keeps moving sideways at the same speed!

---

### 🧲 The "Elevator" Trick:
> Imagine the projectile is in an **elevator moving horizontally at constant speed**. Inside, the ball just goes straight up and comes straight down. That's the vertical component. The horizontal movement is the elevator moving forward. Both happen *simultaneously* but *independently!*

---

### 📝 Formula Memory Mnemonics:

```
T = 2u sinθ/g    →  "Two Ugly Snakes Guard"  (2, u, sin, g)
H = u²sin²θ/2g  →  H has TWO sin's and a 2 below
R = u²sin2θ/g   →  R has sin of DOUBLE angle (2θ)
```

### ⚡ Quick Relationship:
$$R = 4H\cotθ \quad \text{and} \quad T^2 = \frac{8H}{g}$$

---

## 5. ✏️ Example Problem (NEET-Style)

### Question:
> A ball is projected with a velocity of **20 m/s** at an angle of **30°** with the horizontal. Find:
> (a) Time of flight
> (b) Maximum height
> (c) Horizontal range
> *(Take g = 10 m/s²)*

---

### ✅ Solution:

**Given:**
- u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°, g = 10 m/s²
- sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = √3/2 ≈ 0.866
- sin 60° = √3/2 ≈ 0.866

---

**Step 1: Find components**
```
uₓ = u cosθ = 20 × cos30° = 20 × (√3/2) = 10√3 m/s
uᵧ = u sinθ = 20 × sin30° = 20 × 0.5 = 10 m/s
```

---

**Step 2: Time of Flight (T)**
$$T = \frac{2u\sinθ}{g} = \frac{2 × 20 × \sin30°}{10} = \frac{2 × 20 × 0.5}{10}$$
$$\boxed{T = \frac{20}{10} = 2 \text{ seconds}}$$

---

**Step 3: Maximum Height (H)**
$$H = \frac{u^2\sin^2θ}{2g} = \frac{(20)^2 × (\sin30°)^2}{2 × 10} = \frac{400 × 0.25}{20}$$
$$\boxed{H = \frac{100}{20} = 5 \text{ metres}}$$

---

**Step 4: Horizontal Range (R)**
$$R = \frac{u^2\sin2θ}{g} = \frac{(20)^2 × \sin60°}{10} = \frac{400 × \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{10}$$
$$\boxed{R = \frac{200\sqrt{3}}{10} = 20\sqrt{3} ≈ 34.6 \text{ metres}}$$

---

**Verification Check** ✓
```
Also: R = uₓ × T = 10√3 × 2 = 20√3 ✓ (Both methods match!)
```

---

## 🔖 Quick Revision Card

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║           PROJECTILE MOTION — NEET SNAPSHOT          ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  T = 2u sinθ/g      → depends on vertical only      ║
║  H = u²sin²θ/2g     → depends on vertical only      ║
║  R = u²sin2θ/g      → depends on BOTH components    ║
║  Max R at θ = 45°   → R_max = u²/g                  ║
║  Same R: θ & (90-θ) → complementary angles          ║
║  At top: speed = u cosθ (minimum, not zero!)         ║
║  Trajectory = Parabola always

# Uniform Circular Motion (UCM)
### Class 11 | Chapter 4: Motion in a Plane | NEET Physics

---

## 1. 🧠 Core Concept & Definition

**Uniform Circular Motion** is the motion of an object moving along a **circular path** with a **constant speed**.

> ⚠️ Key Distinction: Speed is constant, but **velocity is NOT constant** — because direction changes continuously.

Since velocity changes → there IS acceleration → there IS a net force acting on the body.

### What's Changing vs. What's Constant:

| Quantity | Status | Reason |
|----------|--------|--------|
| Speed | ✅ Constant | Magnitude unchanged |
| Velocity | ❌ Not constant | Direction changes |
| Acceleration | ❌ Not constant | Direction changes |
| Kinetic Energy | ✅ Constant | Speed is constant |
| Angular velocity (ω) | ✅ Constant | Uniform motion |

---

### The Direction of Acceleration & Force:

The acceleration in UCM always points **toward the center** of the circle.
This is called **Centripetal Acceleration**.

> 🎯 "Centripetal" = Center-seeking (from Latin: *centrum* = center, *petere* = to seek)

The force causing this = **Centripetal Force** (also directed toward center).

---

## 2. 📐 Key Formulas

### 🔹 Angular Velocity (ω):
$$\omega = \frac{\theta}{t} = \frac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi f$$

- T = Time period (time for one full revolution)
- f = Frequency (revolutions per second)

---

### 🔹 Linear Speed (v):
$$v = r\omega = \frac{2\pi r}{T}$$

---

### 🔹 Centripetal Acceleration (aᶜ):
$$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r = \frac{v^2}{r}$$

**Direction** → Always toward the center (centripetal)

---

### 🔹 Centripetal Force (Fᶜ):
$$F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r$$

> ⚠️ **NEET TRAP**: Centripetal force is NOT a new type of force. It is provided BY existing forces:
> - Tension (stone in a string)
> - Gravity (moon around Earth)
> - Normal force (car on a curved road)
> - Friction (car turning on flat road)

---

### 🔹 Time Period & Frequency:
$$T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}$$
$$f = \frac{1}{T}$$

---

### 🔹 Relationship Summary:
```
ω → v = rω → aᶜ = v²/r → Fᶜ = mv²/r
```

---

## 3. 📝 Common NEET Question Patterns

### Pattern 1: Finding centripetal acceleration or force
> *"A particle moves in a circle of radius 0.5 m with speed 2 m/s. Find centripetal acceleration."*
→ Direct formula application: aᶜ = v²/r

---

### Pattern 2: Direction of velocity/acceleration
> *"In UCM, which quantity remains constant?"*
→ Remember: **Speed, KE, angular velocity** remain constant; velocity, acceleration, momentum do NOT.

---

### Pattern 3: What provides centripetal force?
> *"A car moves on a curved road — what provides centripetal force?"*
→ **Friction** between tires and road

---

### Pattern 4: Doubling radius or speed
> *"If speed is doubled, radius kept same — what happens to centripetal force?"*
→ Fᶜ = mv²/r → F becomes **4 times** (v² dependence!)

---

### Pattern 5: Vertical circles (advanced)
> *"A stone is whirled in a vertical circle — minimum speed at top?"*
→ At top: mg = mv²/r → v_min = √(gr)

---

### ⚡ Concept Questions Often Asked in NEET:
- Work done by centripetal force = **ZERO** (force ⊥ displacement always)
- Centripetal force and centrifugal force are **NOT action-reaction pairs**
- In UCM, the **net tangential acceleration = 0** (speed doesn't change)

---

## 4. 🧠 Memory Tips & Analogies

### Analogy 1: The Hammer Throw Athlete
When an athlete swings a hammer in a circle:
- **String tension** = Centripetal force (toward athlete's hand = center)
- If string breaks → hammer flies **tangentially** (not outward, not inward!)
- This proves: velocity in UCM is always **tangential** to the circle

---

### Analogy 2: Earth & Moon
Moon orbits Earth in (approximately) UCM:
- **Gravity** = Centripetal force
- Moon doesn't fall to Earth OR fly away → perfect balance!

---

### 🔑 Memory Formula Chain:
```
"Oscar Visits All Films Twice"
ω → v → aᶜ → Fᶜ → T
```

### Golden Rules to Remember:
> 1. **Speed constant ≠ Velocity constant**
> 2. **Centripetal force does ZERO work**
> 3. **Velocity is tangential; Force is radial (centripetal)**
> 4. **No centripetal force = No circular motion (object moves in straight line)**

---

## 5. 💡 Example Problem (NEET Style)

**Question:**
A stone of mass 0.5 kg is tied to a string of length 1 m and whirled in a horizontal circle with a speed of 4 m/s. Calculate:
(a) Angular velocity
(b) Centripetal acceleration
(c) Centripetal force

---

**Solution:**

**Given:**
- m = 0.5 kg
- r = 1 m
- v = 4 m/s

---

**(a) Angular Velocity:**
$$\omega = \frac{v}{r} = \frac{4}{1} = 4 \text{ rad/s}$$

---

**(b) Centripetal Acceleration:**
$$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \frac{(4)^2}{1} = \frac{16}{1} = 16 \text{ m/s}^2$$

*(Direction: toward the center of the circle)*

---

**(c) Centripetal Force:**
$$F_c = ma_c = 0.5 \times 16 = 8 \text{ N}$$

*OR directly:*
$$F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{0.5 \times 16}{1} = 8 \text{ N}$$

*(This force is provided by the **tension** in the string)*

---

**Answer:** ω = 4 rad/s | aᶜ = 16 m/s² | Fᶜ = 8 N ✅

---

## 📌 Quick Revision Box

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         UCM — NEET CHEAT SHEET              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ v = rω          (linear & angular speed)    │
│ aᶜ = v²/r = ω²r (centripetal acceleration) │
│ Fᶜ = mv²/r      (centripetal force)         │
│ T = 2πr/v       (time period)               │
│ Work by Fᶜ = 0  (force ⊥ velocity)         │
│ Velocity → tangential                       │
│ Force → centripetal (inward)               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

> 💬 **Pro NEET Tip:** Every year, NEET asks 1-2 questions on UCM — mostly conceptual (direction of quantities, what remains constant) + one numerical. Master both and you won't lose these marks! 🎯

### The Range Formula
For projectile motion, the horizontal range is:
$$R = \frac{v^2 \sin(2\theta)}{g}$$

### Finding When Ranges Are Equal
For two different angles to give the same range:
$$\sin(2\theta_1) = \sin(2\theta_2)$$

Using the property of sine function: **sin(A) = sin(B) when A + B = 180°**

$$2\theta + 2\theta_2 = 180°$$
$$\theta + \theta_2 = 90°$$
$$\theta_2 = 90° - \theta$$

---

## Verification

Let's check with a numerical example:
- **At θ = 30°:** sin(2 × 30°) = sin(60°) = √3/2
- **At θ = 60°:** sin(2 × 60°) = sin(120°) = √3/2 ✓

(Notice: 30° + 60° = 90°)

---

## Why Other Options Are Wrong

| Option | Why Wrong |
|--------|-----------|
| (A) 45° + θ | sin(2(45° + θ)) ≠ sin(2θ) in general |
| (B) 180° − θ | sin(2(180° − θ)) = sin(360° − 2θ) = −sin(2θ) ≠ sin(2θ) |
| (D) 90° + θ | sin(2(90° + θ)) = sin(180° + 2θ) = −sin(2θ) ≠ sin(2θ) |

---

## Key Concept to Remember 🎯

**Complementary Angle Rule for Projectile Range:**
Two angles θ and (90° − θ) give the **same range** when projected with the same initial velocity.

This is why 30° and 60°, or 15° and 75°, all give identical ranges!
